newsitem.title: UK: British opposition piles pressure on government.
newsitem.headline: British opposition piles pressure on government.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party vowed on Thursday to do its utmost to topple the government but stopped short of promising a no-confidence vote next week.

"Rest assured, we want to get rid of this government and the first opportunity (that arises), we'll do that. But we have to get the rest of the political parties to support us," deputy Labour leader John Prescott told BBC radio.
"If we could bring down the government yesterday or today, we would do it."
Labour, riding high in pre-election opinion polls, plans a parliamentary bid on Monday to sack Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg for his handling of the Mad Cow crisis.

If it wins that so-called censure vote, the opposition might then turn up the pressure another notch and push for a full no-confidence vote in Prime Minister John Major's government, now without an overall majority.
Prescott said his party would "judge all other measures" after Monday night's vote, refusing to say if it would stretch to a no-confidence vote later in the week.
"We can only put down our motion. That's what we've done and we'll be pressing it very hard," he said.

Major must call an election by May 22. A no-confidence motion could trigger that election as early as March, with the Conservatives trailing badly in the polls and very much on the defensive. The BBC said the cabinet planned to examine ways of fighting off such a vote at talks on Thursday.
The Conservatives, in office now for 18 years, were incensed by the renewed threat to their hold on power.
Home Secretary Michael Howard called Monday's vote "a thoroughly opportunistic attempt" to reap political capital out of a farming crisis that has cost lives, jobs and money.

"This is a party without any principle, without any scruple that is prepared to say anything or do anything to get its hands on the levers of power. It is an absolutely nauseating spectacle," Howard told BBC radio.
In order to defeat the government, Labour needs every single opposition vote plus the support of one Conservative rebel.
Early indications showed disquiet on opposition benches about Labour's latest parliamentary tactics.

Prescott conceded Labour could not rely on full support from the centrist Liberal Democrats or Ulster Unionists, who might seek assurances on the Northern Ireland peace process in return for supporting the government.
"You know (how it is) with the Ulster Unionists, they go on negotiating and talking right up to the moment you have the vote," Prescott said.
While the arithmetic is not yet in the opposition's favour, Major's position would be precarious if he loses on Monday.
The prime minister's favoured date for an election is May 1, just three weeks before the final electoral deadline.

But, with Labour some 20 points up in polls, there is daily speculation Major may call the election earlier to avoid a forecasted defeat in a parliamentary by-election scheduled in the Wirral, northwest England, on February 27.
